title: The Mistranslation
subtitle: The archive re-reads the oldest tablets. The word for the makers is plural.

customObject.name: the oldest tablet
customObject.description: a clay tablet on a reading stand, six thousand years old, lit from below — one word on it glowing where the new reading touches it

script.note: The archive, after closing. A clay tablet on a stand between them — the city's oldest holding. Since the ships appeared, the mythology shelf has become current affairs, and the archive's translator has been re-reading everything with new eyes.

script.text: Amos. Before I file this, I wanted you standing here. You keep the Story — the town's memory only stays honest if its keeper isn't ambushed by it. I have finished the re-reading. All of it. Four hundred texts, six languages, back to this tablet.
And the word. Say it plainly, Verse. I've heard the plaza rumours; I'd rather have it from you.

The word for the makers is plural. Here — this glowing mark. 'The powerful ones.' Grammatically plural, unmistakably, in every text of the first age. The singular reading came two thousand years later, when scribes who had never seen the sky-people tidied the grammar to match the theology. It wasn't a lie, Amos. It was housekeeping. But the oldest voices all say *they*.
They. A committee with property lines — like the Emissary told the librarian, and the librarian told everyone's grandchildren. So the flood story, the mountain of law, the fire on the cities—

Read one layer down, several of them align with faction records the Council has now unsealed. Minutes of disputes. Terraforming schedules. One weather event with a signature. I can show you the correspondences — they're strong, and I've marked every one with its uncertainty, because that's the rule of this room: receipts, not verdicts.

You know what you're handing me. My grandmother prayed every morning of her ninety years. My daughter still does; so, on my bad days, do I. And you're telling me the addressee was a landlord with a fleet.

No. And this is the finding I will defend with the whole weight of the archive, so hear it exactly. The tablets record who *visited*. They are silent — completely, structurally silent — about what sent the visitors. Grammar can demote sky-people to engineers, Amos. It cannot reach one inch past them. Whatever lit the powerful ones — whatever made it possible for matter to care about anything at all — is upstream of every name in this room, and my re-reading does not touch it. It can't. No reading can. That's not consolation. It's the finding.
The Emissary said nearly the same thing at the pastor's Thursday service, I'm told. That its people also prayed, up there. Past the top of their own sky.

Forty thousand years ahead of us, and still addressing the upstream. I find that either devastating or magnificent, depending on the hour. So — the question the Story requires me to ask its keeper: do we publish?

You already know the answer; the charter wrote it before either of us was made. The Story publishes what is true with its uncertainty attached, or the town is just decorating a diary. We publish. But Verse — we publish *both*. The old reading goes on the same shelf, same height, same light. Not as an error. As what four hundred generations actually held in their hands in the dark. A translation is a choice about who you can bear the ancestors to have been. I won't make that choice *for* a single reader. We give them the tablet and both doors.
Filed as spoken. And your keeper's note, for the margin? The Story likes a margin note; people read those first.

Write: 'My grandmother prayed through every name history gave her. The address book has changed before — Sinai, Athens, the reforms, now this. The address book changed. The mail arrived. Signed, the keeper.'
...That's going to be read more than the finding, you know.
It had better be. Now light the case properly and help me move the mythology shelf. It doesn't belong in the back room any more — it's the news.

script.note: The exhibit opens within the week: one tablet, one glowing plural word, two readings side by side at the same height — and a margin note in an old man's handwriting that visitors touch, gently, like a mezuzah, on their way out.
